title: Pattersquash Island
summary: A Mastic Neck place name in Unkechaug homelands tied to island, creek, meadow, and tract names in the Pattersquas landscape.
map_geometry_source: Approximate modern Pattersquas historic marker / Pattersquash Creek vicinity based on Tooker location and public marker coordinates; not an exact historical island or tract boundary.
why_this_matters: According to traditional beliefs recorded in the Nesaquake Tales, Pattersquash Island marked the exact coastal location where the seemingly bottomless inland waters of Lake Ronkonkoma secretly connected to the Great South Bay. Recognizing these long-standing geographic narratives reveals how Indigenous communities understood Long Island's diverse water systems as a unified, deeply interconnected ecological network.
introduction_content: Pattersquash is connected with a small island opposite a creek of the same name at Mastic Neck in Brookhaven.
oral_history_content: Pattersquash Island is used by the Unkechaug as a sacred place for initiation ceremonies and vision quests. The island is directly south of the Poospatuck Reservation in Mastic.
history_content: The placename belongs to the Mastic Neck and Moriches Bay landscape within Unkechaug homelands. Land, missionary, and name-origin details appear in the historic moments below.
legends_and_lore_content:
Pattersquash is mentioned in the published Nesaquake Tales compiled by Rufus B. Langhans 1;

The Indians are credited with believing that the lake was bottomless and connected with the Great South Bay at a place called by them Pattersquash. "Pattersquash" translated becomes "little round place."

The Indians, and some whites too, believed that a body which sank in Ronkonkoma came up at Pattersquash. The body even became a white body at times and at other times that of a Negro.
translation_content:
The early forms may connect with a personal name, Paterquam. A related Connecticut comparison suggests a possible reading connected with a small round place, hill, wigwam, or sweat house, but the interpretation remains uncertain.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place names and the stories behind them define how we perceive and connect to landscape.”

— B. ‘Toastie’ Oaster, How place names impact the way we see landscape (2022), Opening section, paragraph beginning ‘Place names and the stories behind them’
whereintheworld_content: Approximate/general point near the Pattersquas historic marker and Pattersquash Creek area on Mastic Neck. This is not an exact historical island, tract, or meadow boundary.
